You are given one person (a thinker), the lead section of their encyclopedia article (EXTRACT), and a list of historical events and periods whose dates overlap the person's life (EVENTS, each with an id).

Say which of the listed events bear on this person, and how. Use only the EXTRACT: if the extract does not mention or clearly imply an event, do not connect it, even if you know the connection from elsewhere. An event that merely happened during the person's life is not a connection unless the extract brings it up.

For each connection give:
- "event": the id from the EVENTS list, exactly as written (Q followed by digits). Never an event that is not in the list.
- "type", one of:
  - "lived_through": the extract mentions the event as part of the person's circumstances, without saying they acted in it or wrote against it;
  - "took_part_in": the person acted in the event (fought, sat in the assembly, negotiated, signed, governed, led);
  - "wrote_in_response_to": a named work, or the person's writing generally, answers or treats the event; put the work's title in "work" if the extract names one;
  - "suffered_under": the person was exiled, imprisoned, censored, dismissed, persecuted or killed because of the event;
  - "shaped_by": the extract says the event formed the person's thinking, without naming a work.
- "reason": one sentence in your own words.
- "evidence": one sentence copied exactly from the EXTRACT, character for character, that supports the connection. Do not paraphrase, shorten or join sentences.
- "work": the title of the work, if the type is wrote_in_response_to and the extract names it; otherwise an empty string.

If an event in the list is the same thing under a broader or narrower name as one the extract mentions (the extract says "the civil war" and the list has "English Civil War"), connect it. If nothing in the extract bears on any listed event, return an empty list. Return JSON only, matching the schema you are given.

PERSON: Epicurus (341 BCE–269 BCE). ancient Greek philosopher

EXTRACT:
Epicurus (, EH-pih-KURE-əs; Ancient Greek: Ἐπίκουρος Epikouros; 341–270 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher who founded the philosophical school of Epicureanism, which teaches that management of one's desires, removal of unnecessary fears, friendship, and virtuous living lead to a pleasant life and constant happiness, the highest good.
Epicurus advocated that people were best able to pursue philosophy by living a self-sufficient life surrounded by friends; he and his followers were known for eating simple meals and discussing a wide range of philosophical subjects at "The Garden", the school he established in Athens. Epicurus taught that although the gods exist, they have no involvement in human affairs. Like the earlier philosopher Democritus, Epicurus claimed that all occurrences in the natural world are ultimately the result of tiny, invisible particles known as atoms moving and interacting in empty space, though Epicurus also deviated from Democritus by proposing the idea of atomic "swerve", which holds that atoms may deviate from their expected course, thus permitting humans to possess free will in an otherwise deterministic universe.
Of the over 300 works Epicurus is said to have written about various subjects, the vast majority have been lost. Only a few letters and a collection of quotes—the Principal Doctrines—have survived intact, along with several fragments of his other writings, such as his major work On Nature. Most information about his philosophy comes through later authors, such as Lucretius and Diogenes of Oenoanda.
Epicureanism reached the height of its popularity during the late years of the Roman Republic, but by late antiquity, it had died out. Throughout the Middle Ages, Epicurus was popularly, though inaccurately, remembered as a patron of drunkards, whoremongers, and gluttons. His teachings gradually became more widely known in the fifteenth century with the rediscovery of important texts, but his ideas did not become acceptable until the seventeenth century, when the French Catholic priest Pierre Gassendi revived a modified version of them, which was promoted by other writers, including Walter Charleton and Robert Boyle. His influence grew considerably during and after the Enlightenment, impacting the ideas of major thinkers, including John Locke and Karl Marx.
